reception.text: The Albuquerque Morning Journal ran the news under the headline "GOVERNMENT PROTECTS GILA CLIFF DWELLINGS."
The Deming Graphic praised the proclamation in an editorial paragraph as a wise act in the interest of archaeological science.
No notice in the national press has been found.
reception.source: Chronicling America search, November 16 to December 31, 1907

political_impact.text: The monument grew out of Gila Forest Supervisor R. C. McClure's December 1906 report recommending a fence and gate across the mouth of Cliff Dweller Canyon.
political_impact.source: Peter Russell, Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument: An Administrative History, ch. 1

political_impact.text: Guarding the monument became an unfunded, incidental duty of a forest ranger stationed seventeen miles away.
political_impact.source: Peter Russell, Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument: An Administrative History

legacy.text: The proclamation protected a site already thoroughly looted within six years of its first recorded visit in 1878, but it kept the ground out of private hands for good.
legacy.source: Peter Russell, Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument: An Administrative History

legacy.text: A nominal custodian was appointed only in 1942, and the first full-time ranger arrived in early 1963.
legacy.source: Peter Russell, Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument: An Administrative History

legacy.text: In June 1924 the Forest Service set aside the surrounding backcountry as the Gila Wilderness, which it calls the world's first area of land designated as wilderness.
legacy.source: U.S. Forest Service, Gila National Forest

today.name: Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument
today.note: Now 533 acres in two units; the only park system unit with Mogollon sites.

related.note: The 1905 proclamation for the Gila Forest Reserve, within which the monument lay.

later_actions.text: Executive Order 6166 (signed June 10, 1933) transferred the monument from Agriculture to the Interior Department.
Kennedy's Proclamation 3467 added about 375 acres, including the detached TJ Ruin unit, and removed the monument from Forest Service administration.
A cooperative agreement returned day-to-day management to the Gila National Forest, with the Park Service keeping jurisdiction.
later_actions.source: Peter Russell, Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument: An Administrative History

uncertain: Whether any lawsuit or formal objection followed is not known; court records were not searched.
Whether the Silver City newspapers reported the proclamation cannot be tested, since their 1907 issues are not digitized.
Whether the Forest Service relied on McClure's report alone in drawing the monument is not known.
The current division of management between the Park Service and the Forest Service should be confirmed with the park.
